---
title: "Calibration curves (4.4 and 4.5)"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("_prepare.R")
box::use(show = projlib/show, util = projlib/msdial_utils)
tr <- tut$to_report
# The normalization with the lowest QC RSD% (the app's default choice) and its first batch
mat_id <- util$mat_id_of_blank_subtracted(tr[["best normalization"]])
batch <- tut$proc[[mat_id]][[1]]
rd <- SumExp::row_df(batch$concn)
# A compound with a valid curve and samples above the LLOQ, preferably one whose linear range
# ends below its highest calibration level (to show the ULOQ)
ok <- rd$has_proper_range %in% TRUE & rd$to_export %in% TRUE
pick <- which(ok & rd$uloq < rd$max_c_conc)[1]
if (is.na(pick)) pick <- which(ok)[1]
fid <- rownames(rd)[pick]
cmp <- rd[fid, ]
in_log <- isTRUE(tr$params$log_calibration)
```

For every targeted compound (`Quant` in the MS-DIAL comment), QuaNTA fits a calibration curve to
the calibration samples (`Cal…` classes) and uses it to turn the signal of every sample into a
concentration. Section 4 of the app shows the curves one compound at a time: choose the compound in
table **4.2**, and figures **4.4** and **4.5** follow.

The examples below show **`r cmp$feature_name`** in batch `r names(tut$proc[[mat_id]])[1]`.

## 4.4 The calibration points

```{r}
#| label: fig-points
d <- SumExp::as_tibble(batch$calcurve[fid, ]) |>
  dplyr::rename(.cc_pt = c_conc) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Batch = as.character(batch_id), .uloq = dplyr::coalesce(uloq, Inf),
    # The place of each point, as in the app
    c_type = dplyr::case_when(
      .cc_pt == lod & .cc_pt == lloq & .cc_pt >= min_c_conc & .cc_pt <= max_c_conc ~ "LOD = LLOQ",
      .cc_pt >= min_c_conc & .cc_pt <= max_c_conc & .cc_pt > .uloq ~ "Above the ULOQ",
      .cc_pt >= min_c_conc & .cc_pt <= max_c_conc ~ "Within limits",
      .cc_pt == lod ~ "LOD",
      .cc_pt == 0 ~ "Cal0",
      TRUE ~ "Out-of-range"
    )
  )
show$plotly_calcurve_points(d, mat_id, title = cmp$feature_name, log_scale = in_log,
                            x_title = "Calibrant concentration", y_title = "Signal (normalized, blank-subtracted)",
                            lod = cmp$lod, lloq = cmp$lloq, uloq = cmp$uloq)
```

Each point is one injection of a calibration sample: its spiked (nominal) concentration on the
x axis and its measured signal on the y axis. Points of the same concentration are replicates; with
several batches, the symbol tells the batch.

**How to read it**

- **Colours** tell the role of each level:
  - *Cal0* (red): the zero calibrant. Its signal gives the thresholds of the LOD (3×) and the LLOQ
    (10×, or the mean plus 3 / 10 standard deviations).
  - *LOD* (blue): the lowest level whose mean signal is above the LOD threshold.
  - *Within limits* (green): the levels the curve is fitted on, from the LLOQ upwards.
  - *Above the ULOQ* (olive): levels in the curve but above its linear range.
  - *Out-of-range* (grey): levels not used for the curve.
- **Shading**: dark grey below the LOD, light grey below the LLOQ, and olive above the ULOQ (dashed
  line), the top of the linear range.
- **Replicates should lie close together.** A level with widely spread replicates is a sign of a
  pipetting or injection problem; with the RSD% option, the LLOQ level must have an RSD% of at most 20%.

## 4.5 The samples on the curve

```{r}
#| label: fig-samples
show$plotly_calcurve_samples(batch$concn[fid, ], batch$calcurve, util$mat_id_in_calibration(mat_id),
                             tut$class_colors, log_scale = in_log)
```

The line is the fitted calibration curve (`r sub("_div_", "/", cmp$calcurve_model[[1]]$best_model_name)`
for this compound). The black points are the calibration samples, the coloured ones the QCs and the
study samples by class, placed at the concentration the curve gives them.

**How to read it**

- **Samples in the white area** are within the calibration range and quantified.
- **Samples in the grey areas** are below the LLOQ (light) or the LOD (dark). Depending on the
  setting *Replace values below the LOD/LLOQ*, their concentrations are replaced (LLOQ/2 or LLOQ/4)
  or reported as *n.q.* / *n.d.*.
- **Samples in the olive area** are above the ULOQ: within the curve but above its linear range, or
  extrapolated above its highest level. Treat these values with care, or dilute and re-measure.
- **A curve far from its calibration points**, or points bending away at the top, suggests that the
  linear range is shorter than the calibration range; see the notes in table 4.2 and the option
  *Enforce linear range*.

::: {.callout-tip}
## In the app
Use the arrow keys ↑ / ↓ in table 4.2 to step through the compounds; both figures follow at once.
With the processing option *Log scale for calibration curve fitting*, both figures have log axes,
which show the low concentrations better.
:::
